text: The last skill this course teaches isn't an algorithm -- it's how to write up what you found, honestly and completely, in a way someone else could verify and trust. This lesson closes the capstone, and the course, by modeling that writeup using the Number Partitioning results from the last two lessons.

Every honest optimization writeup needs five sections. State the problem precisely, with its real-world interpretation in one sentence. Show the QUBO and its Ising conversion, verified, not asserted. List every method tried with its actual result, not just the best one. State plainly which method won by which metric, flagging anything that makes the comparison less than fully fair. And document limitations and costs specifically.

'It was slow' is not a usable limitations statement. Specify instead: the gamma-beta search used hundreds of classical function evaluations, each simulating the full quantum state. Given the true optimum's roughly 0.95% measurement probability, the geometric-distribution expectation says you'd need about 105 shots on average just to observe it once -- compared to LPT's single deterministic pass. A reader should be able to reconstruct the actual computational burden from your numbers, not just rank the methods qualitatively.

Vague limitations sound like 'quantum methods might do better with more qubits.' Precise limitations name the specific untested variable and cite related evidence: 'this result used a depth-1 circuit; Lesson 9 showed depth-2 substantially improved approximation ratio on a different problem, so testing higher depth here is a natural next step this capstone didn't pursue, with no guarantee it would raise the true optimum's probability specifically rather than just lowering expected cost further.'

That's the whole course: combinatorial optimization and QUBO formulation, QAOA, VQE, real quantum finance applications, and a benchmarking discipline that refuses to oversell what hasn't been proven. Every result in this course was computed directly and checked, not asserted -- the same standard your own capstone, and any quantum optimization claim you encounter from here on, should be held to.
